questions.explanation: True. K-fold splits the data into K disjoint parts; in each round one part is the validation set and the remaining K − 1 parts are the training set. questions.prompt: You want to standardize features and then evaluate with cross-validation. Why should you write cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model), X, y, cv=5) instead of standardizing all of X first and then passing it to cross_val_score?

If you standardize all of X first, the mean and std were computed including the validation part, so its information leaks into every fold and the CV score becomes optimistic. A Pipeline does not make things run faster, and it does not use the statistics of the whole dataset.

So the scaler uses the mean and std of the whole dataset for consistency across folds

items.body:
## Evaluation Metrics

### The Confusion Matrix — the Root of All Classification Metrics

| | Predicted + | Predicted − |
|---|---|---|
| **Actual +** | TP | FN (Type II error) |
| **Actual −** | FP (Type I error) | TN |

### Four Classification Metrics

| Metric | Formula | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | (TP+TN)/total | What percentage did we get right? |
| Precision | TP/(TP+FP) | When the model says positive, how often is it right? |
| Recall | TP/(TP+FN) | Of the truly positive cases, how many did the model find? |
| F1 | 2PR/(P+R) | Balances both |

### Choose the Metric by the Cost of Errors

The deciding question: **which error is more expensive?**

| Problem | More expensive error | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| Cancer screening | Missing a case (FN) | **Recall** |
| Spam filtering | Wrongly blocking an important email (FP) | **Precision** |
| Fraud detection | Both are costly | **F1** |

**Why F1 uses the harmonic mean** rather than the arithmetic mean: with P = 1.0 and R = 0.0, the arithmetic mean gives 0.5 (sounds acceptable), while F1 gives **0** — accurately reflecting that the model is useless. F1 does not let you hide a poor metric.

### Metrics for Regression Problems

| Metric | Characteristics |
|---|---|
| MAE | Mean of the absolute errors. Easy to understand, same unit as the output |
| MSE / RMSE | Squares the errors — **penalizes large errors heavily** |
| R² | Compared with the baseline "always predict the mean". 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the baseline |

Choose MAE when all errors are equally bad; choose RMSE when one large error is much more dangerous than many small errors.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))
```

### The Most Common Mistake

**Reporting accuracy alone.** On imbalanced data, a model that always predicts the majority class achieves very high accuracy without detecting a single case of the class you are looking for.

lessons.description: A more reliable evaluation than a single train/test split.

items.body:
## Cross-Validation

### The Problem with a Single Split

A single train/test split gives you **one** number. But that number depends on where the data happens to land. Change `random_state` and the result can jump from 0.74 to 0.81 — even though the model has not changed at all. So which number is the real one?

### K-Fold: Split into K Parts and Rotate

With K = 5: split the data into 5 equal parts, then repeat 5 times — each time take one part as the validation set and use the other 4 parts for training. Finally, average the 5 results.

Every data sample is used for validation exactly once, and for training K−1 times.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, x_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="f1")
print(scores)                        # 5 numbers
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())   # the mean and the spread
```

**The standard deviation matters as much as the mean.** A mean of 0.80 with a standard deviation of 0.02 is a stable model. A mean of 0.80 with a standard deviation of 0.15 means the result depends heavily on how the data is split — it is not yet trustworthy.

### Stratified K-Fold

For classification problems, always use the stratified version so that each fold keeps the correct class proportions. Scikit-learn does this automatically when you pass a classifier to `cross_val_score`.

### Choosing K

| K | Tradeoff |
|---|---|
| 5 | Fast and usually good enough — a reasonable default |
| 10 | More stable estimate, twice as slow |
| = number of samples (LOO) | Least biased but very slow, only suitable for small datasets |

### The Most Common Mistake

**Normalizing the data before running cross-validation.** The scaler has then learned from the entire dataset, including the part that will serve as the validation set in each round — so the result looks better than reality. How to avoid it: wrap the scaler and the model in a `Pipeline`, then pass that pipeline to `cross_val_score`.

items.body:
## Hyperparameter Tuning

### How Parameters and Hyperparameters Differ

| | Parameter | Hyperparameter |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides | The model learns it from the data | **The user sets it** before training |
| Examples | The coefficient `w` of linear regression | `max_depth`, `C`, `n_estimators` |

### Grid Search

List the values you want to try; the library runs every combination and picks the best one according to cross-validation.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

grid = {
    "model__max_depth": [3, 5, 10, None],
    "model__n_estimators": [100, 300],
}
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(x_train, y_train)

print(search.best_params_)
print(search.best_score_)
```

**Note the count:** 4 × 2 = 8 combinations, and each combination runs 5 folds → **40 model trainings**. The wider the grid, the cost grows exponentially.

### Random Search — Often More Effective

Instead of trying everything, draw N random combinations. It sounds worse, but in practice it is often better for the same computational budget: most hyperparameters have little effect, so grid search spends a great many runs probing values that change nothing.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe, grid, n_iter=20, cv=5, random_state=1009)
```

### The Biggest Trap

If you tune based on the test set and then report the result on that same set, that number is **no longer honest** — you have chosen the model that fits the test set best. The correct workflow:

1. Split train / test right from the start
2. Tune with cross-validation **on the training set only**
3. Run the test set exactly once, with the model you have settled on

### The Most Common Mistake

**Running a huge grid from the very beginning.** Run a coarse search over a wide range first to find a good region, then run a fine search around that region — this saves hours of computation.

## Applying the Complete Machine Learning Workflow

This lesson ties together everything you have learned into a single workflow.

### Nine Steps

| # | Step | Question to answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define the problem | What are we predicting? Regression or classification? |
| 2 | Collect data | Is there enough? Does it represent reality? |
| 3 | Explore (EDA) | What is the distribution? How much is missing? Are there outliers? |
| 4 | Split train/test | Do we need to stratify? |
| 5 | Preprocess | Impute, normalize, encode — **fit on train only** |
| 6 | Baseline | A simple model as a point of comparison |
| 7 | Train and tune | Cross-validation on the training set |
| 8 | Final evaluation | Run the test set **once** |
| 9 | Interpret and deploy | How does the model go wrong? Is that acceptable? |

### Complete Skeleton Code

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix

data = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
target = "Outcome"
x, y = data.drop(target, axis=1), data[target]

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1009, stratify=y)

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler",  StandardScaler()),
    ("model",   RandomForestClassifier(random_state=100)),
])

grid = {"model__max_depth": [5, 10, None], "model__n_estimators": [100, 300]}
search = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5, scoring="f1", n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(x_train, y_train)

y_pred = search.best_estimator_.predict(x_test)   # the test set is run ONCE
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))
```

### Step 9 Is the Step Most Often Skipped

Getting a `classification_report` does not mean you are done. Keep asking:

- Which **kind** of error does the model make more often — FP or FN? Is that kind acceptable in the real-world context?
- On **which group** does it go wrong? A model that is 85% accurate overall but only 60% accurate on a specific user group is a fairness problem, not a technical one.
- Does the real data at deployment look like the training data?

### The Most Common Mistake

**Stopping at the accuracy number.** A model is used by real people to make real decisions. Understanding where it goes wrong matters as much as how often it is right.

## 3.P4 Standardization with StandardScaler

**After this unit you will:** standardize data correctly with `StandardScaler` without leaking test data.

### Key points

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
x_train = scaler.fit_transform(x_train)   # fit ONLY on the training set
x_test = scaler.transform(x_test)         # the test set is only transformed
```

| | Formula |
|---|---|
| Standardization (z-score) | `z = (x − u) / s` where `u` is the mean and `s` is the standard deviation |

- `fit_transform` learns the mean/std **from the training set** and then applies them to that same set; `transform` only applies the parameters that were already learned.
- After standardization, `x_train` and `x_test` become NumPy arrays with shapes `(614, 8)` and `(154, 8)`.
- If you also fit on the test set, information from the test set leaks into the standardization step and the evaluation results look better than they really are.

questions.explanation: False — and this is the most common mistake. Only `x_train` is fitted. Fitting on `x_test` leaks information from the test set into the standardization process.

questions.prompt: After standardization, x_train has shape (614, 8) and x_test has shape (154, 8). What is the total number of rows in the two sets?
questions.explanation: 614 + 154 = 768, exactly the number of rows in the original data: standardization neither adds nor removes any rows.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines of code in the correct order for the standardization cell.
questions.explanation: Split into train/test first; create the scaler; fit_transform on the training set (this is where the scaler learns its parameters); finally, transform the test set with that same scaler.

options.label: x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=1009)

questions.prompt: After running x_train = scaler.fit_transform(x_train) and x_test = scaler.transform(x_test), every column of x_test has a mean of exactly 0.
questions.explanation: False. A mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 hold only for x_train, because the scaler learns the mean and std from the training set. The test set is transformed with those same parameters, so its mean deviates from 0. For example, if the scaler learned from the training set [10, 20, 30] (mean 20, std ≈ 8.16), a test value of 40 becomes about 2.45. If you try to force the test mean to 0 by fitting on the test set, information from the test set leaks into the standardization step.

questions.prompt: Why do we use scaler.fit_transform(x_train) but only scaler.transform(x_test)?
questions.explanation: The standardization parameters (mean, std) must be learned ONLY from the training set. If you also fit on the test set, information from the test set leaks into the model and the evaluation results are no longer honest — the model looks better than it really is.

options.label: Because the test set does not need standardization
Because fit_transform can only be run once per session
Because the standardization parameters should be learned only from the training set, avoiding information leakage from the test set
Because the test set is smaller, so there is not enough data to fit

items.body:
## 3.P5 Training a Random Forest and Predicting

**After this unit you will:** train a scikit-learn model, predict on the test set, and know what you need in order to evaluate it.

### Key points

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=100)
model.fit(x_train, y_train)      # learn from the training set
y_pred = model.predict(x_test)   # predict for the test set

report = classification_report(y_test, y_pred, output_dict=True)
```

- The workflow for every scikit-learn model: **create the object → `fit` → `predict`**.
- `fit` only receives the training data (`x_train`, `y_train`); the model must never see `y_test`.
- `y_pred` holds one predicted label for **each row** of `x_test` (154 rows).
- `classification_report(y_test, y_pred)` compares the true labels `y_test` with the predicted labels `y_pred`.

quizzes.title: Quiz 3.P5 — fit and predict
quizzes.description: 5 questions on fit, predict, and the order of the commands.

questions.prompt: Which method of model is used to train the model on the training data? (write the exact method name)
questions.explanation: `fit`, for example `model.fit(x_train, y_train)`.

questions.prompt: The model is trained with model.fit(x_test, y_test).
questions.explanation: False — the model learns from the training set: `model.fit(x_train, y_train)`. If it learns from the test set, there is no "unseen" data left for an honest evaluation.

questions.prompt: x_test has 154 rows × 8 columns. How many predicted labels does y_pred = model.predict(x_test) contain?
questions.explanation: `predict` returns one label for each row of `x_test`, so there are 154 labels.

questions.prompt: Arrange the commands in the order they are executed in the lab session.
questions.explanation: Train (`fit`) → predict (`predict`) → evaluate (`classification_report`). You cannot evaluate before you have `y_pred`.

questions.prompt: You create model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=100) and immediately call y_pred = model.predict(x_test) without calling fit. What happens?
questions.explanation: scikit-learn raises a NotFittedError because the model has not learned anything from the data: `predict` can only be used after `fit`. It does not return random labels, and it certainly does not fit itself on x_test; if it did, the model would have seen the test set. The correct order: create the object, `fit` on the training set, then `predict`.

options.label: It automatically fits on x_test and then predicts
It raises a NotFittedError because the model has not been trained
It returns all 0 labels without raising an error
It returns random labels without raising an error

questions.prompt: In classification_report(y_test, y_pred, output_dict=True), what are y_test and y_pred, respectively?
questions.explanation: `y_test` holds the true labels of the test set (the answers); `y_pred` holds the labels the model predicts for `x_test` via `model.predict(x_test)`. The report compares these two against each other.

options.label: The true labels of the test set and the labels the model predicts for x_test
y_test is the predicted labels, y_pred is the true labels
The labels of the training set and the labels of the test set
Two copies of the same label array

items.body:
## 3.P6 Reading the Evaluation Results

**After this unit you will:** read the precision, recall, f1-score, and support of each class and cross-check them against the confusion matrix.

### Key points

| Class | precision | recall | f1-score | support |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (no disease) | 0.79 | 0.88 | 0.83 | 100 |
| 1 (disease) | 0.71 | 0.56 | 0.62 | 54 |
| accuracy | | | 0.77 | 154 |

- `confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)` gives `[[88, 12], [24, 30]]`, in the order `[[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]`.
- Class 1: a precision of 0.71 means that when the model says "disease", it is correct 71% of the time; a recall of 0.56 = 30 / (30 + 24) means the model finds only 56% of the true disease cases.
- **An accuracy of 0.77 hides the weakness on class 1** — for a disease-screening problem, missing nearly half of the disease cases (24 cases) is serious.
- Ask yourself: is a recall of 0.56 acceptable?

quizzes.title: Quiz 3.P6 — Reading the Classification Report
quizzes.description: 5 questions on reading the evaluation table and the confusion matrix.

questions.prompt: In the classification report, class 1 has a precision of 0.71 and a recall of 0.56 (support 54). What does this tell you about the model?
questions.explanation: Precision 0.71: when the model says “disease”, it is correct 71% of the time. Recall 0.56: but it finds only 56% of the true disease cases — that is, it misses nearly half. For a medical problem, this is a serious weakness.

options.label: The model predicts class 1 almost perfectly
The model produces too many false alarms for class 1
Accuracy is already 0.77, so these two metrics do not matter
Most “class 1” predictions are correct, but the model misses nearly half of the true class 1 cases

questions.prompt: From the matrix [[88, 12], [24, 30]] in the order [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]], compute the recall of class 1 = TP / (TP + FN). (round to 2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: 30 / (30 + 24) = 30 / 54 ≈ 0.56 — matching the class 1 recall of 0.56 in the report table.

questions.prompt: Because accuracy reaches 0.77, we can conclude that the model detects disease cases (class 1) well.
questions.explanation: False — accuracy pools both classes, and class 0 makes up 100 of the 154 rows. The recall of class 1 is only 0.56: the model misses 24 of the 54 true disease cases.

questions.prompt: Adding up all the cells of the confusion matrix [[88, 12], [24, 30]] gives the number of rows in the test set. What is it?
questions.explanation: 88 + 12 + 24 + 30 = 154, matching the `support` of 154 on the macro avg and weighted avg rows (100 + 54).

questions.prompt: In this lesson's classification report (confusion matrix [[88, 12], [24, 30]]), the number 54 in the support column of class 1 is the number of samples the model predicts as class 1.
questions.explanation: False. Support is the number of samples that ACTUALLY belong to that class: 24 + 30 = 54 (the second row of the matrix). The number of samples the model PREDICTS as class 1 is 12 + 30 = 42 (the second column), which is the denominator of precision = 30/42. Confusing these two numbers leads to mixing up the denominators of precision and recall (recall uses 54).

questions.prompt: confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred) gives [[88, 12], [24, 30]] (rows = true label 0 then 1; columns = predicted label 0 then 1). What does the number 24 in the second row, first column mean?
questions.explanation: The second row is true class 1 (disease), and the first column is predicted class 0 (no disease). So 24 is the number of disease cases the model missed (False Negatives) — which is also why the recall of class 1 is only 30/(30+24) ≈ 0.56.

options.label: 24 non-disease cases that the model predicts as disease
24 disease cases that the model predicts correctly
24 cases that truly have the disease but that the model predicts as no disease
24 non-disease cases that the model predicts correctly

quizzes.title: End-of-Course Knowledge Check — Fundamental of Machine Learning
quizzes.description: 15 self-assessment questions covering all three modules.

questions.prompt: The grade column has a minimum value of 2 and a maximum of 10. After Min-Max normalization, what does the value 8 become?
A feature has a mean of 60 and a standard deviation of 5. After z-score standardization, what does the value 70 become?
What type of feature is shirt size S – M – L?
questions.explanation: S, M, L are categories WITH an order (S < M < L), so they are ordinal. Nominal categories have no order (for example, colors).

questions.prompt: The color column has 4 distinct values (black, blue, white, green). After one-hot encoding, how many binary columns will there be?
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates one binary column for each category, so there are 4 columns.

questions.prompt: When standardizing data with a scaler, which approach is correct?
questions.explanation: Fit only on the training set (learn the mean/standard deviation from the training set), then use that same scaler to transform both the training and test sets. Fitting on the test set leaks information from the test set into the model.

options.label: Fit again separately on the test set
Fit on the entire dataset before splitting
Fit on the training set, then transform the training and test sets

questions.prompt: What type of problem is Logistic Regression used for?
questions.explanation: Despite the word regression in its name, it is a classification model: it outputs a probability in the range (0, 1) and then compares it with a threshold (usually 0.5) to decide the label.

options.label: Reducing the dimensionality of the data
Classification, with the output being a probability in (0, 1)

questions.prompt: A decision tree node has 5 samples labeled Yes and 5 samples labeled No. What is the Gini = 1 − Σ pᵢ² of that node?
A branch of a decision tree has Gini = 0. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: Gini = 0 means the branch is completely pure: all samples have the same label, so there is no need to split further.

options.label: The branch is pure: all samples have the same label
The branch is empty, with no samples
The branch has as many Yes samples as No samples

questions.prompt: In an SVM, which points are the support vectors?
questions.explanation: Support vectors are the data points closest to the decision boundary (the margin); only they determine the position of the hyperplane, and points farther away have no influence.

options.label: All points of the positive class
The points closest to the decision boundary
The points farthest from the decision boundary

questions.prompt: How does bootstrapping (the foundation of Random Forest) sample the data?
questions.explanation: Bootstrapping is sampling WITH replacement: an observation can be chosen multiple times in the same sample, and some observations are not chosen at all.

options.label: Splitting the data into equal groups
Sampling with replacement from the original data
Taking exactly the first half of the data

questions.prompt: A classification model has TP = 30 and FP = 10. What is Precision = TP / (TP + FP)?
The same model has TP = 30 and FN = 20. What is Recall = TP / (TP + FN)?
With Precision = 0.75 and Recall = 0.6, what is the F1 score = 2·P·R / (P + R)? (round to 2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 × 0.75 × 0.6 / (0.75 + 0.6) = 0.9 / 1.35 ≈ 0.67. Note that F1 lies closer to the smaller value (0.6), unlike the arithmetic mean of 0.675.

questions.prompt: In a dataset with 99% normal samples and 1% fraud, a model that always predicts "normal" achieves 99% accuracy. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data: this model catches no fraud cases at all (the Recall of the fraud class is 0) yet still has high accuracy. You need to look at Precision, Recall, and F1.

options.label: The model is very good because accuracy is high
The model is good if Precision equals 1
Accuracy is misleading; the model is useless because it misses every fraud case

questions.prompt: A regression model is off by +3 on the first sample and −4 on the second sample. What is the RMSE? (round to 2 decimal places)
questions.explanation: MSE = (3² + (−4)²) / 2 = 25 / 2 = 12.5; RMSE = √12.5 ≈ 3.54. (The MAE on the same data is 3.5 — RMSE is larger because it penalizes large errors more heavily.)

misconceptions.name: Assuming high accuracy means a good model
misconceptions.description: The learner believes high accuracy always means a good model, overlooking imbalanced data where the model simply predicts the majority class.

misconceptions.name: Confusing underfitting with overfitting
misconceptions.description: The learner reverses the diagnosis: a very low training error with a high test error is overfitting (high variance); only when both training and test errors are high is it underfitting (high bias).

misconceptions.name: Thinking bootstrapping never repeats elements
misconceptions.description: The learner confuses sampling with replacement with data splitting or sampling without replacement, and so believes an element cannot appear twice.

misconceptions.name: Believing a more complex model is always better
misconceptions.description: The learner assumes that increasing complexity (polynomial degree, tree depth) always improves results, forgetting that it raises variance and can make test error worse.

misconceptions.name: Treating F1 as the average of Precision and Recall
misconceptions.description: The learner computes F1 as (P+R)/2 instead of 2PR/(P+R), and so does not see F1 being pulled down when one of the two metrics is low.

misconceptions.name: Training the model on the test set
misconceptions.description: The learner calls fit on x_test and y_test, which defeats the purpose of the test set because the model has already seen the answers.

misconceptions.name: Fitting the scaler on the test set
misconceptions.description: The learner uses fit_transform on the test set as well, leaking information from the test set into the scaling step.

misconceptions.name: Calling fit or fit_transform on the test set
misconceptions.description: The learner believes an imputer or scaler should "adapt" to the test set itself with fit_transform, when it should be fit on the training set only and then used to transform the test set; otherwise, statistics from the test set leak into the workflow.

misconceptions.name: Thinking every tree in the forest learns from the same data
misconceptions.description: The learner believes the trees in a Random Forest are all trained on the identical full training set, and so cannot understand why they differ.

misconceptions.name: Confusing False Positives with False Negatives
misconceptions.description: The learner swaps the roles of the prediction and the actual value when naming the cells of a confusion matrix (confusing Type I with Type II errors).

misconceptions.name: Thinking a higher Gini is better
misconceptions.description: The learner believes the feature with the largest Gini is the one to split on, when Gini measures impurity, so a lower value means a purer node.

misconceptions.name: Looking only at the mean and ignoring the standard deviation
misconceptions.description: The learner reads cross_val_score results using only the mean; a large standard deviation shows that scores vary strongly between folds, so the mean is not yet trustworthy.

misconceptions.name: Thinking the kernel trick reduces dimensions
misconceptions.description: The learner understands the kernel trick backwards: believing it reduces dimensions or removes points, rather than lifting the data into a higher-dimensional space.

misconceptions.name: Assuming KFold shuffles data by default
misconceptions.description: The learner believes KFold picks samples at random; in fact shuffle=False, so the folds are consecutive chunks, which causes serious errors when the data is ordered by label.

misconceptions.name: Putting the label column in the feature vector
misconceptions.description: The learner counts the target/label column (for example price) as part of the feature vector or in the number of input features.

misconceptions.name: Assuming low training error means a good model
misconceptions.description: The learner looks only at training error; a model that memorizes even the noise can reach a training error near 0. Training must be compared with test, and the gap between the two numbers is the warning sign.

misconceptions.name: Thinking MAE is more sensitive to outliers than RMSE
misconceptions.description: The learner reverses the relationship: RMSE squares the errors, so it penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE, which makes RMSE the metric that is more sensitive to outliers.

misconceptions.name: Confusing the median with the mean
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks SimpleImputer(strategy='median') produces the arithmetic mean, or does not see that outliers pull the mean off while the median stays put.

misconceptions.name: Confusing missing values with wrong formats
misconceptions.description: The learner puts an empty-cell error (missing value) and an error where a value is present but written in the wrong type (wrong data format) into the same category.

misconceptions.name: Treating any feature made of digits as numerical
misconceptions.description: The learner classifies a feature by how it is stored (digits) rather than by its meaning: province codes, student IDs, and phone numbers are stored as numbers but only identify things, with no order or meaningful arithmetic.

misconceptions.name: Thinking duplicating rows makes data more diverse
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks copying existing samples increases the diversity of the data; in fact it only creates duplicate rows and adds no new information.

misconceptions.name: Thinking SimpleImputer recognizes '?' as missing
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks an imputer recognizes symbols like '?' or 'N/A' as empty cells; by default it treats only NaN as a missing value, so those symbols must be converted to NaN first.

misconceptions.name: Thinking MAE does not depend on scale
misconceptions.description: The learner believes MAE is a unitless ratio; in fact MAE has the same unit as the target variable, so changing units changes MAE, and it cannot be compared across problems with different scales.

misconceptions.name: Ignoring the effect of outliers on Min-Max
misconceptions.description: The learner does not see that a single outlier stretches x_max − x_min, squeezing normal values close together near 0 after Min-Max (or mistakes the formula for x / x_max).

misconceptions.name: Thinking more data fixes every kind of error
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks adding more samples always reduces test error; more data mainly reduces variance (overfitting), while high bias caused by a model that is too simple requires more complexity.

misconceptions.name: Thinking noise-related error can be eliminated entirely
misconceptions.description: The learner believes a powerful enough model or enough data will bring test error close to 0; the random noise in the data (irreducible error) cannot be predicted by any model.

misconceptions.name: Thinking R² always lies in [0, 1]
misconceptions.description: The learner does not realize that R² = 1 − (model error)/(baseline error) can be negative when the model is worse than a baseline that always predicts the mean.

misconceptions.name: Thinking supervised learning can find labels on its own
misconceptions.description: The learner believes a supervised algorithm can run on unlabeled data, overlooking the labeling step (the annotator), which is a prerequisite input.

misconceptions.name: Treating validation and testing as one step
misconceptions.description: The learner uses the same set both to compare and tune models and to report the final score, so the reported score is too optimistic; the test set must be data that was not used for learning or selection.

misconceptions.name: Confusing the units of MSE and RMSE
misconceptions.description: The learner forgets that MSE is in the squared unit of the target variable, while RMSE (the square root) has the same unit as the target variable and can be interpreted directly.

misconceptions.name: Confusing normalization with standardization
misconceptions.description: The learner mixes up the Min-Max formula (scaling to [0,1]) with z-score (mean 0, standard deviation 1).

misconceptions.name: Using ordinal encoding for unordered features
misconceptions.description: The learner assigns the numbers 0, 1, 2... to categories with no natural order (such as colors), unintentionally creating a false order for the model.

misconceptions.name: Mixing up the denominators of Precision and Recall
misconceptions.description: The learner uses TP+FN as the denominator of Precision, or TP+FP as the denominator of Recall.

misconceptions.name: Thinking random_state makes the model more accurate
misconceptions.description: The learner believes that changing or setting random_state improves model quality, when it only fixes the random split so that experiments can be repeated.

misconceptions.name: Confusing regression with classification
misconceptions.description: The learner misclassifies a problem that predicts a continuous value as a classification problem, and vice versa.

misconceptions.name: Thinking RMSE can be smaller than MAE
misconceptions.description: The learner thinks RMSE can be smaller than MAE. In fact RMSE is always greater than or equal to MAE on the same data, and they are equal only when all absolute errors are identical.

misconceptions.name: Thinking sigmoid directly outputs the label 0 or 1
misconceptions.description: The learner believes the output of the sigmoid is simply 0 or 1, skipping the step of comparing the probability with a threshold to produce the label.

misconceptions.name: Thinking every point determines the SVM hyperplane
misconceptions.description: The learner believes that removing any point would change the hyperplane, rather than only the support vectors closest to the margin determining it.

misconceptions.name: Choosing hyperparameters with the test set
misconceptions.description: The learner uses the score on the test set to choose a model or hyperparameters and then reports that same score, making the estimate too optimistic; the test set may be used only once, at the final step.
